Confidence in Hormuz has been 'crushed' by war on Iran, IEA says
The US-Israeli war on Iran has “crushed” confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable waterway for the export of energy, Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), has warned.
“I don’t see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026,” Birol wrote for The Economist magazine in an essay published on Wednesday.
“Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed,” he added.
Birol said that the world "can conceivably manage without the strait," but it would be "difficult".
In its World Energy Outlook report published on Thursday, the IEA said developing alternative pipelines around the waterway would require around $40bn. This would add around $2 to the cost of a barrel of oil exported from the Middle East. An additional $200bn would need to be spent on alternative sources of energy outside the Middle East.
The IEA said that in the case of oil alone, new pipeline projects are under construction or consideration in the Middle East that could pump around seven million barrels per day of oil, allowing producers to reach international markets without going through the strait.

Senate vote to curb Trump war on Iran fails again
For the 15th time this year, the US Senate has tried to curb President Donald Trump's warmaking authority in Iran. It succeeded twice, once in May and once in June, but failed on Thursday by a vote of 51-48.
Fifty Republicans and Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted against the resolution, while only 43 Democrats were present to vote in favour. They were joined by two Independents, and three Republicans in Rand Paul, Lisa Murkowski, and Susan Collins.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who previously voted alongside Democrats, suggested the repeat votes were becoming fruitless, telling reporters on Thursday that there should be "more weight on solving the fundamental problem" instead.
Tillis decided not to run in this month's midterm elections after a spate of Trump-led attacks on him last year. He will now be replaced by Democrat Roy Cooper, the senator-elect, in North Carolina.
The election results were a decisive rebuke of the Trump administration's domestic and foreign policy, as Vice President JD Vance himself acknowledged the very next day.
Trump has previously just ignored the two successful resolutions stipulating that only Congress has the authority to declare - and thereby fund - the US at war.
The move effectively rendered the Senate's efforts moot.

Iraq has reached a compromise with Kataeb Hezbollah, the Iran-backed paramilitary group, three senior security officials told Reuters, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group.
Iraqi officials had accused the Iraq-based group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.
Under the deal brokered by senior Shia political leaders to avert what could have been a civil war, government forces were expected to move into Kataeb Hezbollah stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, according to three security officials familiar with the deal.

A spokesperson for Kataeb Hezbollah said the group's secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, another influential Iran-aligned militia, and other influential figures in a bid to prevent an escalation.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague are scheduled to deliver a judgment on Thursday in a case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority.
If the court rules in Gambia's favour, it will be the first time the United Nations' top court has held a state fully responsible for committing genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
It will be also be the first judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states.
On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court.
Eleven states have intervened, filing submissions on how the Genocide Convention should be interpreted, but mainly in support of the Gambia's case rather than as parties. The states, also present at the court on Thursday, are: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom.
The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.
Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.
Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

The New York Times (NYT) is facing widespread criticism over its report claiming that some of Iran's water infrastructure may have been built to support its missile programme, with critics accusing the newspaper of promoting war propaganda and providing a justification for attacks on Iranian civilian infrastructure.
Published on Monday with the headline "War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason", the article examines the geographical overlap between dam and water infrastructure projects and sites recently struck during the US-Israeli war on Iran. It suggests that some of these projects may have been designed, at least in part, to support military facilities.
One of the two journalists who wrote the piece, Sanam Mahoozi, shared the article on X, writing: “Why has Iran kept building dams amid a severe water crisis? @ErikaSolomon and I examined a striking overlap between water projects and military sites. Could some have served a dual purpose? No conclusive evidence, but questions worth exploring.”
The Iranian Water Diplomacy Association noted on Tuesday "with serious concern" the discrepancies in the report, including the fact that geographical proximity between struck sites and water infrastructure sites does not establish military use.
The report refers to 533 identified dams, but without any statistical analysis, it "has no evidentiary value", the association said. "Historical chronology also does not fit the hypothesis."
"Presenting water infrastructure as military, without credible evidence, blurs the line between civilian objects and military targets in public opinion and normalizes a threat-based view of facilities on which millions depend," the association said in its statement published online.

US judge rules in favour of foreign students and journalists after Trump limits visas
A US federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's attempt to limit visas for international students and members of the foreign press after university and media unions filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in August.
Massachusetts District Judge Dennis Saylor said on Monday that the government has been unable to prove there has been widespread visa fraud or national security concerns with this particular visa programme.
DHS's move to impose restrictions "is arbitrary and capricious", Saylor said in his decision.
"The Final Rule, entitled Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media... is hereby VACATED," he wrote.
Saylor added that DHS is "seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity - providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States - that Congress sought to permit and encourage".
The ruling preserves the "duration of status" or "D/S" stamp that international students receive on their visas and, by extension, on the visas foreign journalists receive as well.
It means they are legally permitted to stay in the country as long as they remain in the status they obtained, either as active students or working journalists, whether it's mere months or several years.

The Tim Hortons app has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertech company founded by alumni of the Israeli military's infamous intelligence Unit 8200, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) has confirmed.
An investigation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) published last week found that the coffee chain app sends data to third-party companies overseas as soon as the app is launched.
Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science at the University of Calgary who scanned the app's network traffic with his team, said the third party built into the app receives enough information to create a digital fingerprint of each device that can be identified later.
Some of the data includes the device's name and unique identifier, details of the device's camera and sensors, and the names of Wi-Fi routers nearby, which can be used to determine the user's location.
"This was beyond the pale," Reardon told the CBC.
Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst, told the CBC that the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service, but the amount of data collected "seems quite excessive" for simply purchasing a cup of coffee.
In its published investigation, CBC did not identify the third party or its location, saying that "accountability rests with the app developer".

In his last phone call with Benjamin Netanyahu as US president, Joe Biden told the Israeli prime minister, "I still love you, pal", according to a transcript of the conversation obtained by the Jerusalem Post.
Five days before leaving office, Biden told Netanyahu, "You're a good man", and "I admire you."

The transript appears to clash with Biden's own account of his relationship with Netanyahu in his memoir Promise Me, America , which has just been published.

Amnesty International called on Wednesday for Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes on el-Obeid in Sudan's North Kordofan state to be investigated as war crimes.
The strikes have hit residential areas and civil infrastructure across the city and its surroundings, killing dozens and disrupting public services.
Amnesty investigated nine RSF drone strikes in el-Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026.
Three of the strikes hit residential areas and four struck key civilian infrastructure, including el-Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market. In all incidents, interviewees told Amnesty they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

A desalination project in water-poor Jordan has drawn investment of $6.7 bn and talks are underway to launch similar projects in Syria and Yemen, the head of the UN's Green Climate Fund told Reuters on Wednesday.
The project is the biggest commitment yet by the world's largest multilateral climate fund. It aims to address water stress at a time when the climate crisis is increasing the problem.
Jordan ranks among the countries with the least available water.
Launched officially on Wednesday by Prince Faisal bin Al Hussein, the younger brother of Jordan's King Abdullah II, the Aqaba–Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project will eventually move 300 million cubic metres of additional water and serve 40 percent of the population.
Last year, the fund approved $295m in grants and loans that attracted further public and private sector funding to reach a total of $6.7bn.
The Green Climate Fund was set up under the United Nations climate framework to help developing nations adapt and curb their emissions.

Trump's Board of Peace says Gaza ceasefire has delivered 'nothing visible'
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, the body supposedly tasked with overseeing the end to fighting in Gaza, has accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to end hostilities, leaving the Palestinian enclave's population in dire need.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a "sobering assessment of progress made since then", Reuters said.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
Since the ceasefire, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,431 people, including at least 300 children, and wounded 5,026.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson for the political office of Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the report.
“There is no ceasefire in Gaza. People talk about a ceasefire but at best it’s a reduced fire,” Chris Sidoti, a member of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told MEE's Expert Witness podcast this week.

Trump lands in China for meeting with Xi and Putin
US President Donald Trump has arrived in China for the Apec summit in Shenzhen, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladmir Putin.
The historic trilateral meeting between the leaders will take place on Thursday. Xi, Trump and Putin are due to meet on the sidelines of the summit to potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran, as well as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.
Xi met Trump off the plane on the tarmac at Shenzhen, reciprocating Trump's gesture when the Chinese leader visited the US in September.
Xi told Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Putin and Trump are unlikely to have time for fully fledged bilateral negotiations in China, but may talk on the event's sidelines, the Tass news agency reported.
Peskov was cited as saying that the two leaders would exchange views on the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran if they got a chance to talk one-on-one.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry has condemned the latest Iranian drone attack on its territory.
The ministry denounced the attacks as "repeated and criminal" and described it as a "direct threat" to the Gulf country's "security and stability".
